lead.t: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are inherited disorders characterized by tumors in multiple endocrine glands, with MEN1, MEN2A, and MEN2B being key examples.

A MEN1 mutation is found in 30–35% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas, highlighting its broader clinical relevance beyond the full syndrome.

Given the high risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma, a RET mutation in MEN2 syndromes necessitates screening of family members, often leading to prophylactic thyroidectomy in carriers to prevent disease progression.
It is crucial to always screen patients diagnosed with phaeochromocytoma for MEN2 syndromes, as it is a common component of these genetic conditions.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are inherited disorders causing tumors in several endocrine glands. The three main types—MEN1, MEN2A, MEN2B—have distinct tumor patterns and genetic mutations that guide screening and management.

sections.p: MEN syndromes are autosomal dominant conditions caused by germ‑line mutations in tumor suppressor genes (MEN1) or proto‑oncogenes (RET). Affected individuals develop hyperplasia or neoplasia in multiple endocrine organs, often at a young age.
b: MEN1 gene on chromosome 11q13 → loss of menin protein.
RET proto‑oncogene on chromosome 10q11.2 → gain‑of‑function mutations.

sections.p: Mutations disrupt normal cell‑cycle control, leading to unchecked proliferation of endocrine cells. Menin normally regulates transcription and DNA repair; RET activation drives MAPK and PI3K pathways.
b: Loss of menin → increased transcription of growth‑promoting genes.
RET activation → constitutive tyrosine‑kinase signaling.

sections.p: Normal endocrine feedback loops (calcium‑PTH, insulin‑glucose, catecholamine‑BP) are overridden by autonomous tumor secretion, causing biochemical abnormalities.
b: Parathyroid hyperplasia → hypercalcaemia, suppressed PTH feedback.
Pancreatic islet tumors → gastrin or insulin excess, independent of gastric pH or glucose.

sections.p: Each MEN type has a characteristic tumor set. Recognising patterns helps prioritize genetic testing and surveillance.
b: MEN1: Parathyroid, Pancreas (gastrinoma, insulinoma), Pituitary.
MEN2A: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Pheochromocytoma, Parathyroid hyperplasia.
MEN2B: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus.

sections.p: Early detection prevents life‑threatening complications such as hypercalcaemic crisis, severe hypoglycaemia, hypertensive emergencies, or metastatic thyroid cancer.
b: Hypercalcaemia → renal stones, neurocognitive decline.
Insulinoma → refractory seizures, coma.
Pheochromocytoma → hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia.

t.b: Is hyperparathyroidism present? Elevated calcium with inappropriately high or normal PTH confirms parathyroid involvement.
Is an insulinoma likely? High insulin with low glucose suggests pancreatic islet tumor.
Is pheochromocytoma present? Elevated metanephrines confirm catecholamine‑secreting tumor.
Is medullary thyroid carcinoma present? High calcitonin is highly sensitive; if unavailable, proceed to ultrasound and fine‑needle aspiration.

sections.p: Focus on inheritance, key tumor triads, and screening steps. Remember that MEN2 requires RET testing and prophylactic thyroidectomy in carriers.
b: MEN1 → 3 Ps mnemonic.
MEN2A → 2 Ps + medullary thyroid carcinoma.
MEN2B → mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus.

faq.a: Clinical pattern + biochemical confirmation + germ‑line genetic testing for MEN1 or RET mutations.
Penetrance is high (≈95 % by age 50) but age of onset and tumor type vary.
Early genetic screening and prophylactic surgery (e.g., thyroidectomy for RET carriers) reduce morbidity and mortality.

exam: List the characteristic tumor triad for each MEN type and the responsible gene.
Explain the biochemical work‑up for a patient with suspected MEN2A.
Describe the management steps for a RET mutation carrier without current disease.
